articles.fullText:
The United States launched new strikes against Iran and Iran-backed groups on Wednesday, as Washington and Tehran continued a cycle of military escalation that has heightened fears of a broader regional conflict.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on social media that US forces had carried out strikes against Iran, calling the operation "a powerful response" to Tuesday's firing by Iran on US bases in Jordan and at ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
The strikes came after US President Donald Trump threatened to hit Iran "hard" in retaliation for Tehran's latest actions.
According to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Iran had earlier targeted a US air base in Jordan with ballistic missiles and halted three "violating" oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. The US and Jordan said the missiles were intercepted.
Following the Iranian attacks, CENTCOM said US and Saudi forces had conducted strikes in Iraq against what they described as "Iran-aligned" targets.
Iraq's paramilitary Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) said on Wednesday that multiple PMF headquarters across several provinces, including Baghdad, Basra and Nineveh, were hit in the US-Saudi strikes, leaving at least 20 people dead and 32 others wounded.
Trump said he had not ruled out further strikes against Iran's regional allies. He also said he hoped to add a provision authorizing tariffs on Iran to a Russia sanctions bill introduced by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, rather than relying solely on sanctions.
Unprecedented US-Saudi strikes raise concerns in Iraq
The US-Saudi strikes in Iraq came despite diplomatic efforts by Baghdad to address tensions.
Iraq's Ministerial Council for National Security condemned the attacks, saying they occurred while the Iraqi government was "actively engaging with the relevant parties" to verify and address concerns raised by both Saudi Arabia and the US over alleged attacks targeting Saudi territory.
Analysts warned that the operation could further destabilize Iraq's fragile political and security balance.
"The Iraqi government has been trying to execute a delicate balancing act between competing regional powers," said Mohammed al-Jubouri, a professor of media at Baghdad-based al-Iraqia University. "These joint strikes risk destroying that neutrality and pulling Iraq deeper into the US-Iran vortex."
The strikes also marked a significant shift in Washington and Riyadh's regional security approach, analysts said, warning that rising tensions with Iran and its allied groups could push the region toward a wider confrontation.
The PMF is a state-sponsored umbrella organization made up of dozens of armed factions. It was formally incorporated into Iraq's armed forces after playing a major role in a campaign against the extremist Islamic State group.
Iraqi international relations expert Nadhum Ali described the joint operation as "a highly dangerous security escalation," saying PMF factions represent one of "Iran's closest proxy networks," and that further retaliation is highly likely.
"The coming days will be critical," said Ali. "If Iran opts for multi-front retaliation through its partners in Iraq, Yemen and Lebanon, the question is whether Washington and Riyadh are truly prepared for the fallout."
The escalation came as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Washington in an effort to increase pressure on Iran.
The two leaders held a nearly 90-minute closed-door meeting on Tuesday focused largely on Iran and its nuclear program, according to statements released by the US and Israeli governments.
A senior Israeli official said on Wednesday that Netanyahu expressed doubts over the possibility of a US-Iran agreement and discussed with Trump ways to increase economic pressure on Tehran through both military and non-military means.
The official said the two sides discussed three options being considered by Trump: continuing efforts to reach an agreement with Iran; maintaining a maritime blockade and increasing economic pressure; or resuming and expanding military strikes.
Trump has expressed concerns that a prolonged conflict could disrupt energy markets and harm the global economy, while Netanyahu argued that Iran was using the Strait of Hormuz – a key global oil route – as one of its remaining leverage points to pressure Washington.
Global oil prices surged on Wednesday amid the latest US-Iran developments and rising geopolitical risks. Both New York crude futures and London Brent crude futures gained more than 7% during trading.
Netanyahu also made clear that Israel would respond if Iran launched attacks against it.
Given that the meeting produced no specific agreements, new cooperation mechanisms or major announcements, some Israeli media outlets analyzed that Washington and Tel Aviv do not have completely identical strategic priorities, with the US seeking to keep the situation under control while Israel wants to maintain pressure on Iran. They also noted that the two sides are maintaining high-level coordination mainly to manage differences rather than establish a new consensus. Besides, despite Israel's efforts to influence American policy, media said the US remains the key player shaping the region's trajectory.
US public grows wary of Iran war
The Trump administration is facing growing pressure to end a conflict that has disrupted the economy and pushed up prices ahead of the November midterm elections.
Public support for the war has declined, with Americans increasingly questioning the objectives of US military involvement.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll released Monday found that only about one-third of Americans support the war against Iran – the lowest level of backing since the conflict began.
The poll, conducted from Friday through Sunday, showed that 69% of Americans, including four in 10 Republicans, believe the administration has not "clearly explained the goals of US military involvement in Iran."

Hamas has approved the latest draft of a roadmap aimed at completing the implementation of the second phase of the Gaza ceasefire agreement, marking a potential breakthrough in negotiations after more than two and a half years of conflict in the enclave.
However, major disputes between Hamas and Israel remain unresolved, particularly over the sequence of key steps, including disarmament, Israel's military withdrawal and Gaza's post-war governance. While Hamas says the transfer of weapons can only take place after Israeli forces withdraw from Gaza, Israel insists that the enclave must be fully demilitarized before any withdrawal.
Analysts caution that Hamas' acceptance of the roadmap does not necessarily indicate a fundamental political shift, but rather reflects its attempt to adapt to the realities of the prolonged conflict. They said the agreement's success will ultimately depend on whether all parties can fulfill their commitments during the implementation process.
Hamas, Israel make contradictory claims
In a statement on Friday, Hamas said it agreed to include discussions on the transfer of heavy weapons within the framework of the Gaza ceasefire agreement, but only on the condition that Israel first ends all forms of military action and withdraws from the Gaza Strip.
According to the statement, the conditions include a complete halt to Israeli military operations, the withdrawal of Israeli forces, the entry and assumption of duties by the Palestinian National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) to handle civil functions, the deployment of international stabilization forces, the dissolution of armed groups and militias established by Israel, the launch of reconstruction efforts and guarantees for Palestinian self-determination and an independent Palestinian state.
Hamas senior official Basem Naim said on the same day that, after intense negotiations, the group had agreed to the latest version of the ceasefire roadmap. He stressed that Israel must fulfill its commitments under the agreement, while mediators and guarantor countries should take responsibility for monitoring and pressuring Israel to comply with the deal and prevent violations.
Israel, however, rejected the proposal, with far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir saying the latest Gaza ceasefire roadmap announced by the so-called "Board of Peace" was "unacceptable."
Ben-Gvir argued that a commitment to halt attacks on Hamas members would effectively allow the group to prepare for another assault.
The Israeli Prime Minister's Office said a day earlier that the current disarmament plan did not meet Israel's requirements, emphasizing that Israeli forces would only withdraw after Gaza was fully demilitarized. Israeli officials said troops would not pull back from their current positions along the "yellow line" until Hamas achieved "genuine disarmament."
Meanwhile, Israeli military operations in Gaza have continued. The Israel Defense Forces said on Friday that recent airstrikes across Gaza had killed two Hamas officials. The military also said it had carried out dozens of operations in the occupied West Bank over the past week, arresting more than 200 Palestinians.
Implementation remains the biggest challenge
"The proposal does not eliminate the fundamental disagreements between the parties," said Esmat Mansour, a political analyst based in Ramallah. "The most sensitive issues have effectively been postponed to the implementation stage, where they are likely to face their most difficult test."
Beyond the dispute over whether withdrawal or disarmament should come first, analysts say the roadmap faces broader challenges, particularly regarding Gaza's future administration and reconstruction.
Under the proposed arrangement, Hamas would transfer governance responsibilities in Gaza to a Palestinian national committee. Palestinian analyst Akram Atallah said the committee would face major obstacles, including securing broad Palestinian support, rebuilding administrative institutions and obtaining sufficient funding for reconstruction.
Meanwhile, the post-war governance mechanism has also encountered difficulties.
The United States announced the establishment of the "Board of Peace" in January to oversee Gaza's transitional administration, but the initiative has faced setbacks. Several US allies, including France, Norway, New Zealand and Italy, reportedly declined to participate. The board has also struggled to secure reconstruction funding, with reports suggesting it had raised less than $1 billion, far below the previously proposed target of $17 billion. In April, reports emerged that the board had yet to enter Gaza due to funding shortages and other obstacles.
While Hamas' approval of the roadmap represents an important political step, the coming months will determine whether the understandings reached through negotiations can be translated into lasting arrangements on the ground.
Li Zixin, a Middle East expert at the China Institute of International Studies, told China Media Group that the agreement could ultimately fail if it does not clearly define Israel's obligations.
"The US-backed phased approach mainly outlines demands on Hamas, while Israel's responsibilities are not clearly specified," Li said. "During implementation, Hamas may accuse Israel of failing to withdraw troops and blocking reconstruction supplies from entering Gaza, while Israel may accuse Hamas of violating the agreement and carrying out attacks. This could eventually lead to renewed fighting and the collapse of the deal."
"The real measure of success will not be the announcement of an agreement, but the ability of all parties to implement every stage of it in accordance with their commitments," Mansour said. "Only then can the roadmap provide a genuine opportunity for long-term stability in the Gaza Strip."

(ECNS) -- A stark contrast is emerging in today's international discourse: on one side, Western politicians relentlessly promote so-called supply chain "de-risking," under the spotlight, introducing one legislative proposal after another. On the other side, markets and businesses are feeling the chill as they confront the cold, hard costs of reality.
A recent estimate by EY-Parthenon found that if the United States, the Eurozone, and the United Kingdom hope to largely eliminate their dependence on Chinese supply chains in key industries by 2050, they would need to invest an additional $23.6 trillion over the next 25 years. The figure places an almost unimaginable price tag on the prolonged push to "decouple from China."
What does $23.6 trillion actually mean? It is equivalent to more than 70% of the annual Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of the United States.
This implies that if Europe and the U.S. insist on a sweeping separation from China's industrial chains, the cost would be extraordinarily high. It would not only impose an unbearable burden on Western businesses but could even place the broader Western economy under severe strain.
More importantly, even if the West were willing to foot this enormous bill and pour such vast sums of money into the effort, ending their reliance on Chinese supply chains in the short term would remain virtually impossible.
In recent years, Washington and Brussels have continued to introduce and expand restrictive measures targeting China's industrial and supply chains .
More recently, the European Union has reportedly been considering broader supply chain auditing rules, in an attempt to pressure European multinational corporations into reducing their reliance on critical Chinese components through mandatory legal instruments.
However, administrative intervention, cannot ultimately override the fundamental forces of the market.
A U.S. financial institution acknowledged in a report on global "nearshoring" that true supply chain restructuring is by no means as simple as "moving a factory." Every cross-border relocation of a production line involves substantial losses in the value of fixed assets, the duplication of supporting infrastructure, and sharp increases in cross-border logistics and compliance costs.
These costs will ultimately be passed on to ordinary consumers in the West as inflationary pressure.
A recent survey of supply chain executives shows that after repeated and costly disruptions, key decision-makers in Western enterprises are being forced to adopt a more pragmatic approach. Given the efficiency, quality, and irreplaceable cost advantages offered by Chinese suppliers, many Western companies have concluded that continuing to prioritize them remains the most commercially rational choice.
This is because Chinese enterprises no longer occupy their places in global industrial chains through simple "low-end assembly." Instead, their technological advantages and deeply developed industrial ecosystems have embedded them within the very capillaries of high-end global manufacturing.
One of the clearest examples is currently unfolding in Morocco, on the shores of the Mediterranean Sea.
To evade tariffs and shorten transport distances, European automotive giants have in recent years touted Morocco as a so-called "nearshoring paradise," attempting to build it into a beachhead for "de-risking" away from China.
However, in-depth investigations by industry media have revealed an ironic reality for European policymakers. No sooner had European automakers established factories in Morocco than Chinese auto parts suppliers followed, embedding their technology and capital within the local supply chain.

The "flood barriers" painstakingly constructed by Western politicians have quickly become little more than leaky sieves when confronted with the powerful forces of technological capability and cost competitiveness.

articles.fullText:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi talks about setting up the National Intelligence Bureau at her office in Chiyoda Ward, Tokyo, Japan, May 27, 2026. 
Japan has taken further steps to strengthen its security apparatus and military capabilities, with the government establishing a new national intelligence agency and conducting its first test launch of a long-range cruise missile, moves that have sparked concerns over the country's accelerating military buildup.
On Friday, the Japanese government officially established the National Intelligence Bureau aimed at enhancing the country's intelligence-gathering capabilities. Hara Kazuya was appointed as the head of the new intelligence agency.
Meanwhile, according to Japan's Ministry of Defense, the country's Self-Defense Forces conducted a test launch of the US-made Tomahawk cruise missile in the Pacific Ocean on July 28, marking Japan's first such test.
The Tomahawk is a subsonic long-range cruise missile typically launched from naval vessels and submarines. Designed mainly for naval deployment, it also has land-based variants, with a maximum range exceeding 2,000 kilometers.
Experts said Japan's recent moves, including strengthening its intelligence capabilities and accelerating the development and deployment of offensive weapons, indicate that the country's postwar principle of "exclusive defense-oriented policy" is increasingly being eroded.
Wang Guangtao, an associate researcher at the Center for Japanese Studies at Fudan University, criticized the establishment of the the intelligence bureau, saying the move would further reinforce a "Prime Minister's Office-led" vertical chain of command, concentrating power while lacking sufficient oversight.
"Japan had a similar vertically structured intelligence system before World War II, which was deeply intertwined with its militarism and overseas aggression," said Wang, adding that "The revival of such an intelligence agency inevitably reminds people of wartime Japan's high-pressure intelligence management system and its suppression of individual freedom of expression."
Cai Liang, a researcher at Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said Japan's efforts to build a centralized intelligence system and strengthen the prime minister-led command structure represent a departure from the constraints of the postwar pacifist framework and could continue to disrupt regional security.
"Japan's intelligence system has moved beyond the traditional defensive framework and is being integrated with national security strategies, providing proactive intelligence support for the development of the Self-Defense Forces' counterstrike capabilities and the expansion of military boundaries," Cai said.
He added that intelligence reform has become a key step in Japan's push to break away from postwar restrictions and build an "intelligence-driven military." Japan's proactive expansion of its intelligence strategy could continue to affect the regional security landscape and deserves close attention, he said.
Japan's recent moves have not only raised nerves among neighboring countries, but have also intensified domestic public concerns over the country's growing military ambitions.
Since the House of Representatives election in February, Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) has used its majority in the lower house to advance a series of security-related legislation, including the act establishing the new intelligence body, despite resistance from opposition parties and criticism from parts of society.
The LDP has also called for increased defense spending as part of its proposal to revise Japan's three key security documents later this year, paving the way for further expansion of the country's defense capabilities.
Japan this year has seen a number of protests, during which demonstrators criticized a series of dangerous policies and bills promoted by Sanae Takaichi's government.
Some protesters accused the government of ignoring public concerns and warned that the current administration is gradually pushing Japan toward war. Others expressed concern that the new intelligence agency could lead to expanded collection of citizens' personal information, threatening privacy and freedom of speech.
